opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way we thought about it was that there was a real shift in where the leverage is. A few years ago, if you wanted a frontier-level system, you basically had to pre-train from scratch, and that meant enormous capital before you'd learned anything about whether your approach worked. What changed is that open-weight base models got good enough that the pre-training step started to look less like a moat and more like a starting point.

Ioannis and I came from working on reinforcement learning at DeepMind. We'd both spent a lot of time on systems like AlphaGo and then on RL for large language models. The lesson from that whole line of work is that the step change in capability comes when you pair a strong prior with reinforcement learning against a real reward signal. Pre-training gives you the prior. RL is what gets you from "knows a lot" to "can actually accomplish the task reliably."

Coding is almost the ideal domain for that, because you have verifiable feedback. Code compiles or it doesn't, tests pass or they fail, and you can run things in an environment and see what happens. That gives you a much cleaner reward than most open-ended domains. So our bet was: take the best available open-weight model, invest heavily in RL infrastructure, environments, and reward design for software engineering, and see how far post-training alone gets you.

It turned out to be very capital-efficient. You can iterate quickly, figure out which parts of the recipe matter, and build real product with customers, all without a giant pre-training bill on day one. And everything you learn about RL and agentic coding carries over. If you later decide to train your own base models, you're doing it knowing exactly what you need from them, rather than spending a huge amount of money and hoping.

So for us it was about sequencing. Start where the signal is clearest and the cost of learning is lowest, prove out the RL side, and earn the right to go deeper down the stack over time.

r001.rationale: The response says open-weight models became good enough that pre-training looked less like a moat and more like a starting point. It does not say pre-training was converging on a known paradigm.

r002.rationale: It mentions the enormous upfront capital of pre-training, but does not argue that extracting more signal from noisy internet data would eventually require prohibitively expensive scaling.

r003.rationale: The response describes RL as capital-efficient and says coding has verifiable feedback, but does not identify manageable RL compute costs as a temporary opportunity for a focused entrant to build a best-in-class coding product.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key insight for us was that the landscape had shifted in a pretty fundamental way. A few years ago, if you wanted to build a frontier coding model, you had no choice but to pre-train from scratch, and that's an enormous capital expense before you've learned anything about whether your approach works. But by the time we started Reflection, you had open-weight models that were genuinely strong base models. The pre-training had, in some sense, been commoditized, at least at the level you need to start from.

And what we'd seen at DeepMind, and what I'd seen working on things like Gemini and the agent work before that, is that the real differentiation increasingly comes from what happens after pre-training. Reinforcement learning is where you take a model that knows a lot about the world and you turn it into something that can actually accomplish tasks reliably. Coding is almost the ideal domain for that because you have verifiable outcomes. The code either compiles, the tests either pass, the agent either completes the task or it doesn't. That gives you a clean reward signal, which is exactly what RL needs to work.

So the bet was essentially: let's not spend the first year and hundreds of millions of dollars reproducing something that already exists in the open. Let's take a strong base and put all of our effort and compute into the post-training stack, the environments, the reward design, the scaling of RL itself. That's the part that's still genuinely hard and where we felt we had real expertise.

Now, I'll be honest that there's a tension in that. You're dependent on someone else's base model, and you don't fully control its characteristics. Longer term I think you want to own more of the stack, and we've thought a lot about when it makes sense to pre-train ourselves. But as a starting point, it let us get to a competitive coding system much faster and much more capital-efficiently than the alternative, and it let us learn what actually matters before committing to the biggest expense.

r001.rationale: The response says strong open-weight models made pre-training effectively commoditized, but does not state that pre-training was beginning to converge on a known paradigm.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss noisy internet data or the prohibitive cost of scaling pre-training to extract further signal.

r003.rationale: It describes concentrating effort on RL and reaching a competitive coding system more capital-efficiently, but does not say RL compute costs were currently manageable or present this as a temporary opportunity to build a best-in-class product.

astra-6.text:
The way we thought about it was that pre-training gives you a very strong starting point, but it doesn’t necessarily give you a system that can do useful work reliably over a long horizon. There’s a lot left to learn between predicting the next token and being able to take a coding task, work through a repository, run tests, and fix your own mistakes.

Open-weight models create an opportunity to focus on that second part without having to fund pre-training from scratch. The bet is that reinforcement learning can contribute a substantial amount of capability on top of that foundation, rather than just making the model’s answers look a little better.

Coding is a particularly good place to pursue that because you can get feedback from the environment. You can execute the code, see whether the tests pass, and train on whether the system actually accomplished the task. The hard part is building the environments and the learning process that turn that feedback into general capability.

So we saw an opportunity to put our resources into that learning loop. You still depend on the quality of the underlying model, but you don’t have to assume that all of the differentiation comes from pre-training.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training provides a strong starting point but leaves work to do; it does not say pre-training was beginning to converge on a known paradigm.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss noisy internet data, diminishing signal, or prohibitively expensive scaling.

r003.rationale: It describes investing resources in reinforcement learning, but does not identify manageable RL compute costs as a temporary opening for a focused entrant to build a best-in-class coding product.

sol-6.1.text:
The way we thought about it was that pre-training gives you this incredibly capable starting point, but it doesn’t necessarily give you an agent that can reliably do a long piece of work. There’s still a lot to learn in that gap, and our bet was that reinforcement learning could do a substantial amount of that learning.

Coding is a particularly good place to pursue that because you can get feedback from the environment. You can run the code, run the tests, and see whether a change actually solved the problem. That gives you a way to train on outcomes rather than just imitate what somebody wrote.

So open weights let us start with a strong foundation without having to build the whole pre-training operation upfront. The opportunity was to take that foundation and ask how far we could push it through reinforcement learning—especially toward systems that can work through problems, recover from mistakes, and keep going. It wasn’t that compute suddenly became free. It was that we could focus our compute and our research on the part where we thought we could make the biggest difference.
